debates.title: Are coding agents now reliable daily drivers?
debates.summary: Simon Willison argues that October 2026 marks a new inflection point where coding agents can reliably build video games, extending the earlier 2025 breakthrough for software development. Nathan Lambert counters that while performance scores rise, creating meaningful benchmarks at the frontier remains difficult, casting doubt on true reliability.

positions.stance: Claims October 2026 is a clear inflection point where coding agents, especially Claude Opus 5.5, can reliably create fun video games
Warns that improving scores is cheap compared to building meaningful benchmarks, so the real reliability of agents is still uncertain

debates.title: Do open‑weight models finally catch up to closed models?
debates.summary: Ethan Mollick points to recent closed‑benchmark results showing open‑weight models lagging behind the frontier, with no Fable‑class open model yet. In contrast, swyx highlights Kimi 3.1 Pro’s open‑weights performance, claiming it reaches Fable‑5.1 level and narrows the gap with closed‑source leaders.

positions.stance: Reports that closed benchmarks reveal open‑weight models falling further behind and that no open model matches Fable‑class performance yet
Flags Kimi 3.1 Pro as an open‑weights model achieving Fable‑5.1‑class results, narrowing the lead of closed models

debates.title: Can experts stay unbiased when AI agents suggest answers?
debates.summary: Ethan Mollick shares findings that experts are subtly swayed by AI positions even when they believe they remain independent, urging deliberate timing of AI assistance. Simon Willison amplifies this concern by urging engineers to document where AI tools fail, framing such documentation as a sign of sound judgement.
